reconstructed_article: The Freewinds, a ship owned by the Church of Scientology, was sealed in April 2008 at Curaçao, where public health officials launched an investigation into the presence of blue asbestos. According to The Daily Herald and Lloyd's List, work on the ship's interior was suspended on April 27 after health inspectors found traces of blue asbestos. Samples taken from paneling were sent to the Netherlands, where analysis revealed levels of blue asbestos. An April 25 inspection involved Frank Esser, interim director of the Curaçao Drydock Company; Christiene van der Biezen, Curaçao's head of labor affairs; Tico Ras, head of the local health department; and two inspectors. Panama Maritime Authority director Alfonso Castillero stated an investigation was underway. Lawrence Woodcraft, a former Scientologist and licensed architect, supervised work on the ship in 1987 and attested to the presence of blue asbestos in a 2001 online statement. He reported his findings to Church of Scientology executives at the time. The Church of Scientology purchased the ship, then known as the Bohème, in 1987 through Flag Ship Trust, and put it into service in June 1988 for advanced Scientology training and spiritual retreats. Church spokeswoman Karin Pouw stated that air quality inspections in April confirmed the Freewinds meets U.S. standards. A team from the United States traveled to Curaçao to remove asbestos. A May 15 statement to a UK newspaper said there has never been asbestos exposure on the Freewinds.

reconstructed_article:
On Friday, 178 plaintiffs, including construction workers and family members of deceased workers, filed a lawsuit in Tokyo, Japan, seeking approximately 6.6 billion yen (about 64 million USD) in damages from the Japanese government and 46 building manufacturers. According to reports, the class action is the first in Japan related to health damages caused by asbestos exposure at construction sites. The plaintiffs are from Tokyo and surrounding areas.

They claim that the government and manufacturers, despite knowing of the dangers of asbestos inhalation, failed to take proper precautions, including ceasing to promote asbestos as a cheap construction material and banning its production. After inhaling asbestos in the workplace, 172 people developed lung cancer or mesothelioma, and nearly half of those afflicted have died.

The plaintiffs argue that the government and health ministry, despite international organizations issuing warnings in 1972 that asbestos could be a carcinogen, did not act quickly enough. They also blame the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry for sanctioning asbestos use under the Factory Act, and the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism for approving asbestos-containing materials under Japan's Building Standards Law.

Approximately 40 construction workers plan to file a similar lawsuit in June. The government, following a 2005 revelation that residents near a factory developed asbestos-related diseases, implemented a 2006 law providing monetary assistance to victims and relatives. reconstructed_article: On Tuesday at approximately 4:00 a.m., around 500 melon-headed whales were spotted struggling near the shores of Pilar, Bataan, approximately 135 kilometers northwest of Manila. Philippine Coast Guard commander Luis Tuazon and Bataan Governor Enrique Garcia Jr. reported the sighting. More than 100 fishermen and volunteers, along with personnel from the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR), local police, and the Coast Guard, deployed dozens of fishing boats with engines shut off in an effort to guide the whales toward deeper waters by clapping and hitting the water surface. The mammals were initially misidentified as dolphins but were later identified as melon-headed whales by local veterinarian Mariel Flores. Four dead whales washed up in Abucay and Tortugas, including two adult females, one pregnant and one that had given birth to a calf that also died. A necropsy by Dr. Lemnuel Aragones of the University of the Philippines found the two adults had damaged eardrums. Provincial veterinarian Alberto Venturina said the adults weighed 250 to 300 kilograms, and the calf was approximately one month old. BFAR director Malcolm Sarmiento Jr. noted this was the worst stranding recorded, with previous events involving only 20 to 30 animals. By 4:30 p.m., the whales were guided back to deeper waters. Possible causes discussed included underwater earthquakes, chemical pollution, dynamite fishing, and a sea floor earthquake study conducted by the Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory. PHIVOLCS reported no significant seismic events at the time.

Business administrator Dana Sullivan said testing on March 31 confirmed asbestos in a brown undercoating of plaster. The affected area was sealed off by district officials. reconstructed_article: The Christchurch Mail Centre in New Zealand was evacuated Friday after employees refused to continue working because of exposure to heavy amounts of dust suspected to be asbestos. Tuam 2 Ltd, the company set to convert the 27-year-old Christchurch Mail Centre into a new city council building, has been aware of the presence of asbestos in the building since May 2008. Hawkins Construction contacted authorities voicing concerns of possible exposure to asbestos material. Testing is currently underway at the facility to determine the nature of the exposure. The Christchurch Mail Centre is operated by New Zealand Post. According to Christchurch Delivery Business Leader Duncan Burman, approximately 50 post workers operate out of the facility, which services about 35,000 addresses in the central Christchurch region. Tony Marryatt, chief executive of the city council, was asked by Councillor Helen Broughton for an explanation of the incident. Broughton, the only councillor who voted against construction of new city council buildings, said she wanted to see the professional opinion from a building consultant who had assessed the building. The owners of the Christchurch Mail Centre informed New Zealand Post that testing performed in November confirmed there was no asbestos in the area. Anna Kenny, a spokesperson for the New Zealand trade union, said concerns were raised about plumes of dust Friday morning suspected to be asbestos, but there has been no confirmation. Kenny confirmed that no asbestos was found in a check of the building in November, but requested further air quality checks before workers return.

Tropical Storm Danielle has intensified into a hurricane with winds up to 130 km/h (80 mph). The storm is headed towards Bermuda, and forecasters at the National Hurricane Center in Miami, Florida expect it to strengthen further over the next two days. Danielle is the second hurricane of the 2010 Atlantic hurricane season. The storm formed near the Cape Verde Islands off the coast of West Africa and was initially classified as Tropical Depression Six. Meteorologists warn Danielle will be the first of several storms to form within the next two weeks, as the Atlantic hurricane season reaches its peak. Rick Knabb of the National Hurricane Center stated, "There are signs that the Atlantic is acting like it should in August and September. We're seeing more activity than we did earlier in the season."

Meanwhile, Tropical Storm Frank, an 80 km/h (50 mph) storm in the Pacific Ocean, is located about 210 km (130 miles) south-southwest of Acapulco, Mexico. Mexico has issued a tropical storm watch for the area. Although the 2010 season appears to have low activity, emergency officials continue to stress safety and awareness to residents in hurricane-prone areas. Lauren McKeague of the Florida Division of Emergency Management said, "It only takes one storm to cause a loss of lives and devastating property damage." Hurricane Andrew was cited as a Category 5 storm that occurred during a lower-than-average season.

GOP presidential candidates Michele Bachmann, Herman Cain, and Mitt Romney sought his endorsement. He endorsed Romney in 2008. The endorsement could help Perry with voters who have had concerns about his record on illegal immigration.

He defended the bill during a September presidential debate, saying those criticizing him “don’t have a heart.” He later backed down from the statement. As Governor of Texas for eleven years, Perry has overseen the state with the longest border with Mexico. He vetoed a bill that would have allowed illegal immigrants to receive driver’s licenses and signed another requiring identification to vote. During his presidential campaign, Perry opposed the proposed full-length border fence, calling it impractical. He favors targeted fencing combined with mobilization of enforcement personnel.

reconstructed_article:
The Australian Government is proceeding with construction of a $210 million, 800-bed detention facility on Christmas Island, about 1,400km off Australia's northwest coast. Construction began in January 2005, and the facility is scheduled to be operational by late 2006. A DIMIA spokesperson said the facility would serve as an immigration reception and processing centre, and that a review of mainland detention centres would likely follow its completion.

Christmas Island Shire President Gordon Thompson said residents were concerned about impacts on tourism, restricted access to fishing and snorkelling areas, and a lack of consultation. He said the Shire council was not notified when the existing Christmas Island detention centre reopened on November 17 to detain seven West Timorese asylum seekers. Azmi Yon, president of the island's Malay association, said locals were seeking written clarification on the facility's purpose.

Democrats senator Andrew Bartlett said transferring asylum seekers to the remote location denied them proper processing and legal access. Greens senator Kerry Nettle called for construction to be suspended, citing existing detention capacity of 3,975 people across facilities including Baxter, Villawood, Maribyrnong, Perth, Port Augusta, Port Hedland, and Woomera.

Environmental concerns were raised because the site is adjacent to Abbott's Booby habitat within Christmas Island National Park. Research indicated that nesting birds within 300 metres of clearings experienced lower breeding success, with 36% of breeding sites in that zone. The Wilderness Society criticised the government's decision to exempt itself from EPBC Act environmental scrutiny.

Colonel Winthai Suwaree expressed a similar sentiment to media. The United States Department of State advised citizens to reconsider non-essential travel to Thailand and avoid protest groups. The junta imposed internet censorship, television broadcast restrictions, and banned political assemblies of five or more people. Some protesters interpreted the gesture as representing freedom, election, and democracy. One pre-war justification was that Iraq possessed weapons of mass destruction, none of which were found. The Senate Intelligence Committee is considering three possibilities: the weapons were moved, CIA intelligence was flawed, or satisfactory intelligence was mishandled by the administration. The last possibility has not been formally investigated.

On Friday, Andy Martin announced via press release that he is seeking the U.S. Republican Party's 2016 presidential nomination, his fourth bid for the White House. Martin, a perennial candidate for political office, is best known for spreading multiple conspiracy theories concerning the background of U.S. President Barack Obama. He previously ran for the Democratic Party presidential nomination and unsuccessfully sought the Republican Party's backing in 2012, when he received 19 votes in the only primary ballot on which he appeared. Martin filed paperwork with the Federal Election Commission last month to officially run for president in 2016, joining 139 other Republican Party presidential candidates who have done likewise.

In his announcement, Martin outlines six reasons for running, including degrading the candidacy of former Florida Governor Jeb Bush, who is also seeking the Republican nomination. Martin aligns himself with fellow Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump, whom he praises throughout the announcement. He positions himself as the "eighteenth candidate," willing to participate in the second-tier debate, and declares himself the "second-most exciting" candidate, reserving first place for Trump. Martin says Trump has the media power to weaken Bush, and that he has the negative information and hardball media tactics to make Bush a toxic candidate for the Republican base. He adamantly opposes Bush because of the foreign policy of the candidate's brother, former President George W. The People's Alliance for Democracy (PAD), a Thai anti-government movement, conducted a disruption campaign designated the “King Taksin operation,” named after an 18th-century Siamese monarch. PAD protesters began gathering on Sunday and besieged the parliament building on Monday morning, forcing the cancellation of joint MP and Senate sessions. The PAD said it would continue disrupting parliamentary sessions until parliament went into recess or the government resigned. The PAD opposes proposed constitutional changes. The government said these changes were not on Monday’s agenda and that ASEAN-related legislation was scheduled instead.

Thailand, the current chair of ASEAN, faced concerns about its ability to ratify treaties at an upcoming meeting in northern Thailand. With parliament inactive, PAD protesters targeted additional government offices, including the temporary cabinet location at the old Bangkok international airport. The government had operated from mothballed buildings there since the PAD forcibly seized the main Government House compound in late August. A PAD call for a public sector strike met with limited response.

The government of Prime Minister Somchai Wongsawat of the People Power Party (PPP) was the target. Authorities avoided confrontation following clashes the previous month in which two protesters were killed when police used tear gas. Police did not intervene as protesters laid siege to the empty parliament building.

Deposed former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra, in self-imposed exile and facing a two-year prison sentence in Thailand, stated in an interview with Abu Dhabi’s Arabian Business that he intended to return to politics. He condemned the UK government for revoking his visa. He was believed to be staying in Dubai.

reconstructed_article: Sam Savarino, developer and CEO of Savarino Companies, confirmed that he has acquired a severely damaged stable and livery on Buffalo's West Side from owner Bob Freudenheim for $1.00 and plans to restore it. The building partially collapsed on June 11, causing 15 homes to be evacuated. Savarino stated he hopes to save the facade, at least 20 feet of the side walls, all of the back walls including the elevator tower, and if possible all three floors. He inherits a tax lien of over $400,000 against the property, which represents the cost the city was billed for limited demolition work performed before the purchase. The city is currently suing Freudenheim to recover those fees. The building is undergoing minor demolition to stabilize the remaining structure. Savarino's plans include living units on two floors with parking on the ground floor. Construction could begin as early as this year, but more likely next year, leaving the timeline uncertain. The project is estimated to cost at least $3,500,000, and all plans must be approved by the city's planning board. The city had originally ordered an emergency demolition after Freudenheim gave permission on June 12 during an emergency Preservation Board meeting, stating he would not rehabilitate the building. Residents obtained a restraining order to halt demolition. The next hearing is scheduled for September 2.

In the ICT category, 388 products were on display from the industry. In total, 308 products from 102 companies were entitled as "Taiwan Excellent Products." Several world-class experts judged the nominated products, selecting the final twenty-nine based on four critical factors. TAITRA also oversaw categories where people could vote over the Internet or using their mobile phones.

ASUSTeK Computer Incorporated picked up two Gold Awards and six Silver Awards and was the biggest winner in the awards. TAITRA presented ASUSTeK Computer Incorporated with the Taiwan Excellence Best Performance Award, while D-Link Corporation received the Taiwan Excellence Achievement Award.

Gold Award winners included the ASUS R700t portable navigation device, AverVision SPB350, N133I6 ultra-slim wide LCD panel, MBA-00 Glee Cube multimedia IP-TV box, P3650 Touch Cruise, Hiwin E2 ecological and economical lubrication module, and Merida Ninety Six carbon full suspension. Silver Award winners included products from ASUS, Gigabyte, Panasonic, D-Link, ZyXEL, Giant, and others across multiple categories.

MusicDNA uses compression methods similar to MP3 and includes an XML file that defines additional content such as lyrics, artwork, tour dates, blog posts, videos, and Twitter feeds. The files also contain audio analysis information intended to improve search, recommendation, and playlist tools. Bach Technology CEO Stefan Kohlmeyer said MusicDNA has been in development since the company was founded in 2007. Bach holds a strategic partnership with Fraunhofer IDMT, and Fraunhofer IDMT CEO Karlheinz Brandenburg, who is credited with inventing MP3, participates in research and development discussions at Bach. According to the article, unlike iTunes LP, MusicDNA is based on open standards and is platform-agnostic, allowing transfer between devices and the purchase of individual tracks rather than full albums. Additional content updates dynamically when the user is online. Only paid files receive dynamic updates, which Bach Technology describes as an incentive to purchase legitimate files instead of using peer-to-peer networks. Mark Mulligan, vice president and research director at Forrester Research, told a UK newspaper that innovations like iTunes LP need to go further and suggested that people should pay once for regularly updated content. Kohlmeyer noted that MP3 was developed more than twenty years ago and, apart from portability, does not add to the listening experience. MusicDNA's rollout is staggered over 2010, with beta versions around Easter and full commercial rollout expected in summer.

reconstructed_article: L. Alan Winters, distinguished professor of economics at the University of Sussex and founding director of the UK Trade Policy Observatory (UKTPO), was interviewed about UK trade policy following Brexit. He said he was opposed to Brexit and considers it poor economic policy, arguing the UK would have been better off with a tighter relationship with Europe to keep trade costs lower. He co-authored reports including "The Costs of Brexit," "COVID-19 will reinforce the Brexit shock," and "Taking stock of the new UK-EU Trade and Cooperation Agreement." Winters said Brexit and COVID-19 shocks interact, making recovery from lost export markets harder. The announcement came after another controller was suspended this week for falling asleep while directing aircraft near [location]. In one incident, two commercial passenger jets landed without direction from the control tower because the controller had fallen asleep.

Under the new plans, controllers must have a minimum of nine hours of rest between shifts, an increase of one hour. More supervisors will be required during night shifts, and controllers will be restricted in what shifts they can swap with colleagues.

LaHood said controllers who fall asleep on duty will face consequences. Earlier this week, the head of the air traffic organization at the FAA resigned after LaHood called the crisis unacceptable. The results of a study on how fatigue affects controllers will soon be published, and the FAA may make further changes. The union representing controllers in the U.S. said it had full support for the new steps.

reconstructed_article: Roger D. Kornberg of the United States was awarded the 2006 Nobel Prize in chemistry for his studies of the molecular basis of eukaryotic transcription. Kornberg's work explains how information encoded in DNA is used to produce the proteins that keep cells functioning. Eukaryotes are multi-celled organisms, such as animals, plants, and fungi, which store their genetic material in nuclei within their cells. To use this genetic information, eukaryotes extract bits of the coded information by forming messenger RNA, which consists of copies of a particular gene within the DNA strand. Translation occurs when proteins are built from the information transcribed in the messenger RNA. Eukaryotic transcription is vital for life; if transcription is interrupted, as can happen when cells are exposed to certain toxins, the cells die. Kornberg documented the process of eukaryotic transcription through snapshots of the process in action. He created the snapshots by crystallizing cellular material partway through transcription and exposing it to x-rays, which produced patterns revealing the intermediate structures. Kornberg's work may lead to novel drugs and medical treatments. Kornberg's father, Arthur Kornberg, received the Nobel Prize in physiology and medicine in 1959 for explaining how organisms synthesize DNA from nucleotides.

reconstructed_article: American botanist Lou Jost has discovered the world's smallest orchid among the roots of a larger plant in a nature reserve in Ecuador. The flowers measure 2.1mm wide and have transparent petals that are only one cell thick. The finding surpasses the previous record held by Platystele jungermannioides, which has 2.5mm flowers. Jost discovered the new species accidentally while examining a larger plant collected from the reserve in eastern Ecuador. The reserve was created by a British organization in partnership with Fundacion EcoMinga, for which Jost works. Ecuador has been the site of discovery of more than 1,000 new orchid species in the past century. Jost said he found the tiny plant among the roots of another small orchid he had collected and taken to his greenhouse to flower. Months later, he noticed the smaller plant among the roots and recognized it as more significant than the larger orchid. He said that examining the flower is often the best method for identifying orchid species and determining whether a specimen is unknown. The newly discovered orchid belongs to the same genus as the previous record holder. It is the 60th new orchid species that Dr. Jost has discovered in the past decade.

Although they measured the approximate temperature of the universe to be about 3.5 kelvins, their ground-based microwave telescope could not pick out the detail available to COBE.

reconstructed_article:
International researchers conducting twin studies carried out parallel genetic investigations into bipolar disorder and schizophrenia, examining more than 50,000 people worldwide. Eleven genetic regions were identified; seven were associated with schizophrenia, five of which had not been previously discovered. Two genetic loci were associated with both diseases. The studies scanned genomes of healthy and affected individuals.

The researchers found that genetic factors are numerous rather than a single faulty gene. In schizophrenia, at most around 30% of genetic components are thought to have been identified.

Pablo Gejman, a lead researcher on the schizophrenia study, said that one goal of genetic research is to find druggable targets. He identified calcium-activated channels in the brain as promising candidates for new drugs, linked to schizophrenia in the study. A genetic locus called mir137 suggests an abnormality of gene regulation. The team found no evidence that dopamine receptors are involved, although current drug treatments target them.

Professor Rodney Scott from the University of Newcastle in Australia praised the strength of the research as lying in its numbers, providing robust statistical power. Both Gejman and Scott commended the study as highly reliable because of its large sample size. Scott noted that the two shared genetic loci were suggestive of a potential common pathway giving rise to both diseases. Gejman called it an excellent and compelling demonstration because the same chains are common to both disorders.

Each illness affects approximately 1% of people. The diseases are poorly understood, and it remains uncertain whether they are components of a single spectrum or comprise multiple illnesses.

The report notes that major gains took considerable time: it took 40 years, from 1870 to 1910, to see major improvements in girls' school attendance aged 6 to 12.

The authors find that U.S. women are disproportionately represented in teaching and nursing, are paid less than male counterparts, and are underrepresented at the highest business levels, with only 28 of Fortune 1000 companies having a female CEO. Women in the bottom 20% economically have a slightly higher birth rate than those in the top 20%. Immigrants from Southeast Asia and India show higher than expected male-to-female birth ratios, which the authors attribute partly to deliberate sex selection based on cultural attitudes.

In 2009, over half a million U.S. women were victims of intimate partner violence. U.S. men hold greater pension assets, and elderly women are more likely to live alone than with a spouse. Guards at the Santa Clara County Jail found Martinez unconscious in a cell with a plastic bag around his neck at approximately 11:19 p.m. on Wednesday. He was taken to a local hospital and pronounced dead early Thursday. Martinez had been incarcerated since January 10 on charges of battery and assault with a deadly weapon.

Martinez first gained public attention in the fall of 1992 for attending classes at UC Berkeley in the nude. He appeared on national television talk shows, where he described his practice as an exercise of free speech and a challenge to sexual repression in Western society. UC Berkeley subsequently expelled Martinez for violating the school's code of conduct, and city officials passed an anti-nudity ordinance.

Family and acquaintances reported that Martinez had experienced undetermined mental illness over the preceding decade without receiving comprehensive treatment. He had moved among halfway houses, psychiatric institutions, and jail during that period. Nearly 1,000 people have been arrested in Iraq as part of a sweeping crackdown against al-Qaeda in Mosul, Iraq's third-largest city. Iraqi security forces have moved into the surrounding countryside to search for more people who fled. The operation is targeting Mosul, described as one of al-Qaeda's most notorious strongholds.

An adviser to the Prime Minister said most of the leaders had fled, some to an unnamed neighboring country. Borders with Syria and Turkey lie about 60 miles from Mosul. The adviser said operations would continue and that the Iraqi army would not leave Mosul until security and stability had been accomplished.

The head of U.S. operations in northern Iraq, who has troops involved in the operation, said he did not believe large numbers were still at large since the operation's Thursday launch, but he conceded that many leaders may have fled before it began to avoid arrest. He said the combination of the arrests and the discovery of a number of weapons caches would reduce the number of attacks in Mosul.

The city is now sealed off by barriers and checkpoints and is being searched by troops; no fighting has been reported. Iraq's Interior Minister reported 1,068 arrests, though only 94 have been cleared and released. Several of those arrested held high- and mid-level positions in al-Qaeda's command structure, including leaders of suicide bomb cells and people who arranged for foreign fighters to enter Iraq.

The Prime Minister has offered amnesty to fighters who surrender their weapons, provided they have not killed civilians.

U.S. federal agents arrested an 11th man on charges connected to a plot by 10 other men to overthrow the government of Laos. A federal grand jury handed down indictments for the 11 men, including former Royal Lao Army general and Hmong leader Vang Pao, 77.

Dang Vang, 48, was arrested at his Fresno home in an early morning raid by agents from the ATF. The men are charged with violating the U.S. Neutrality Act, which outlaws using United States soil to conspire to overthrow a foreign government with peaceful relations with the U.S. U.S. Attorney McGregor Scott said federal law prohibits conspiring to overthrow a foreign government with whom the nation is at peace.

According to the ATF investigation, Dang Vang wrote the group's action plan, summarizing a plot to blow up government buildings in Laos and assassinate government officials. The plot was named Operation Popcorn, or Political Opposition Party's Coup Operation to Rescue a Nation.

Those charged also include Harrison Jack, 60, a retired California National Guard colonel and Vietnam War veteran; Lo Cha Thao, 34; Lo Thao, 53, of Sacramento; Youa True Vang, 60, of Fresno; Hue Vang, 39, of Fresno; Chong Vang Thao, 53, of Fresno; Seng Vue, 68, of Fresno; Chue Lo, 59; and Nhia Kao Vang, 48. Most of those indicted are prominent members of the Hmong immigrant community in California's Central Valley.

reconstructed_article: On May 7, a driver who was not authorised to take the vehicle stole a coach from the yard of private hire operator Dualway. The bus was later located by the coach company, where the driver attempted to run over the son of the owner of Dualway. The driver then returned to the Dualway depot, prompting a response involving up to 20 Garda patrol cars and a police helicopter. The Gardaí fired several shots at the driver's tires in an attempt to stop the vehicle and laid tacks on the road. The bus was driven down the wrong side of the N7, where it collided with a number of cars, killing a female driver, and rammed five Garda patrol cars that were blocking the road. The driver was apprehended and arrested at the Dualway depot after crashing the bus. One person is dead and 13 others, including 5 members of the Garda Síochána, are injured. Sections of the N7 as well as surrounding roads were closed following the incident for forensic examinations, and tram services were severely curtailed.

reconstructed_article:
Matthew Wright, host of British television programme The Wright Stuff, apologised for remarks he made on the show about the murder of Liam Aitchison. During the edition broadcast on Tuesday, Wright said "there's been another murder" in a false Scottish accent, referencing the television crime drama Taggart. Panelist Charlie Baker remarked that the investigation would be like "the longest episode of Taggart of all time," and the audience laughed.

Liam Aitchison's family issued a statement calling the comments "insensitive and offensive" and "very upsetting and insulting for, not just the family, but for the whole community of the Western Isles." His father, Norman Aitchison, wrote on the programme's website that he was "disgusted" and asked whether panel members would joke if it were their own child.

On the following day's broadcast, Wright said he would "like to apologise" if viewers were offended, stating that there was no intention to belittle the tragedy. Channel 5's spokeswoman said Wright's apology was "clear." Wright noted that he had not been helped by campaigns urging people to report him to Ofcom, a UK media regulator, and advised such people to "grow up."

Channel 5 removed Tuesday's episode from its website. Angus MacNeil, MP for Na h-Eileanan an Iar, described Wright's behaviour as "beyond belief" and intended to complain to Ofcom. Comhairle nan Eilean Siar also complained. A Facebook page titled "Report The Wright Stuff to Ofcom" attracted over two thousand likes. Ofcom was assessing complaints but had not decided whether to investigate.

reconstructed_article:
On Thursday, the U.S. House of Representatives voted 269-152 to reject the Net Neutrality Amendment to the COPE Act. The House then passed the COPE Act by a 321-101 vote the same day. The bill is designed to make it easier for telecommunications companies to offer cable TV service and strengthen competition. Proponents said it would lower high-speed Internet prices by enabling providers to bundle phone, data, video, and mobile services. It was the first major telecommunications bill before Congress in over a decade.

The Net Neutrality amendment sought to require broadband providers to treat all data equally, specifying a duty not to block, impair, degrade, discriminate against, or interfere with access to lawful content, applications, or services. Its passage would have prevented companies such as AT&T, Verizon, and Comcast from charging content providers like Google, Yahoo, Amazon, or eBay for priority network access.

Democrats largely supported the amendment, with 140 voting in favor and 58 against, while 11 Republicans voted for it and 211 against. House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi argued that additional fees would burden small web-based businesses and hamper noncommercial communications. Phone companies and Congressional allies argued the restrictions would discourage investment in network upgrades.

The bill is due to be discussed next in the Senate.

reconstructed_article:
Kevin Underwood, 26, a resident of the same apartment complex, became the focus of the investigation after police in Purcell, Oklahoma, about 40 miles (64 km) south of Oklahoma City, discovered the body of ten-year-old Jamie Rose Bolin on Friday in his apartment. McClain County District Attorney Tim Kuykendall said the body was found in a storage bin in the bedroom closet. Underwood was arrested on suspicion of first-degree murder and held without bail. He had no prior criminal record or history of mental illness.

Bolin was last seen on Wednesday near the Purcell public library, and her family reported her missing that night. Officials issued an Amber Alert on Thursday night, noting that no abduction had been reported initially. Underwood drew suspicion at an information checkpoint set up at the apartment complex.

Police found a decorative dagger, hacksaw, barbecue skewers, meat tenderizer, and wooden cutting board in his apartment. Preliminary autopsy reports indicated Bolin died of asphyxiation and blunt force trauma to the head. Authorities said deep saw marks on the body indicated an attempt to decapitate her. Police suspected postmortem molestation, as the body was found unclothed.

Purcell police chief David Tompkins stated the motive appeared to involve a plan to kidnap, rape, torture, kill, decapitate, drain of blood, rape the corpse, eat the corpse, and dispose of the organs and bones. Kuykendall said Underwood reported fantasizing about eating someone beginning a year prior. Authorities believed other individuals, including a woman and a 5-year-old boy, had been targeted and considered. Kuykendall stated he intended to seek the death penalty.

On Tuesday at approximately 4:00 a.m., about 500 melon-headed whales were spotted swimming near the shores of Pilar, Bataan, about 135 kilometers northwest of Manila. Philippine Coast Guard commander Luis Tuazon and Bataan Governor Enrique Garcia Jr. mobilized in response, coordinating an effort to protect the animals. More than 100 fishermen and volunteers, along with personnel from the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR), local police, and the Coast Guard, were deployed by authorities and used dozens of fishing boats with engines shut off to guide the whales toward deeper waters by clapping and hitting the water surface.

The mammals were initially misidentified as dolphins but were later identified as melon-headed whales by local veterinarian Mariel Flores. Four dead whales were found in Abucay and Tortugas, including two adult females—one pregnant and one that had given birth to a calf that also died. A necropsy by Dr. Lemnuel Aragones of the University of the Philippines found the two adults had damaged eardrums. Provincial veterinarian Alberto Venturina said the adults weighed 250 to 300 kilograms, and the calf was approximately one month old.

BFAR director Malcolm Sarmiento Jr. noted this was the largest stranding recorded, with previous events involving only 20 to 30 animals. By 4:30 p.m., authorities and volunteers had successfully guided the whales back to deeper waters. Possible causes discussed included underwater earthquakes, chemical pollution, dynamite fishing, and a sea floor earthquake study conducted by the Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory. PHIVOLCS reported no significant seismic events at the time.

U.S. District Judge Stein ruled that the use of a 25-second clip from John Lennon's song "Imagine" in a film critical of religion is likely defensible under the fair use doctrine. The film, "Expelled," produced by Premise Media and starring comedian Ben Stein, uses the clip to represent what Premise representative Anthony Falzone described at a hearing as "the most popular and persuasive embodiment of this viewpoint that the world is better off without religion." In the song, Lennon proposes the hypothetical "Imagine there's no heaven ... and no religion too."

The report mentions India over 300 times, compared with Spain at 48, Canada at 22, and New Zealand at 15. According to the World Bank, gender equality contributes to productivity, outcomes for the next generation, and representative decision making. In India, improved local-level gender equality correlated with improvements in sanitation, water supplies, irrigation, and schools. Nationally, a woman's income correlated positively with the number of years her children spent in school. Among the richest 20% of Indian families, no gender gap exists in attendance, but among the poorest 20%, males outnumber females 5 to 1. Girls in the bottom 20% average completion of Grade 1, while males average Grade 6. By age 15, parents in Andhra Pradesh prioritize outcomes for male children over female ones. Indian women earn $0.64 for every $1 earned by men, compared with $0.62 in Germany, $0.60 in Georgia, $0.90 in Malawi, $0.82 in Egypt, and $0.80 in Benin and Mexico. India reduced the average number of children per woman from six to three in 35 years, compared with 100 years in the United States. India's maternal mortality rate is six times that of Sri Lanka. Excess female deaths in India dropped by 8,000, from 265,000 in 1990 to 257,000 in 2008; in China they grew by 202,000.

Ministers from thirteen Asian countries pledged on Friday to double the wild tiger population on the continent to 7,000 by 2022. The commitment was made in Thailand at Asia's first ministerial conference on tiger conservation.

The thirteen countries that endorsed the pledge were Bangladesh, Bhutan, Cambodia, China, India, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, Nepal, Russia, Thailand, and Vietnam, all countries where the wild Asian tiger is still found.

In a video address, Thai Prime Minister Abhisit Vejjajiva said the wild tiger is in crisis and that this may be the last chance to save it.

The meeting was partially organized by the Global Tiger Initiative, a coalition within the World Bank, as well as the Smithsonian Institution and various conservation groups.

Meeting host Suwit Khunkitti, Thailand's minister of natural resources and environment, noted that there were 100,000 tigers across range countries 100 years ago, compared with about 3,500 today.

According to the World Wildlife Fund (WWF), tiger numbers have declined due to poaching. The animals live in only seven percent of the territory they occupied a hundred years ago, according to Voice of America.

WWF representative Michael Baltzer said it was important to act during the Year of the Tiger. Global Tiger Initiative program director Keshav Varma said saving the tiger also preserves habitat for other species and draws attention to issues including encroachment and corruption.

The closure of Corus' Teesside operations may be forced by a consortium's refusal to honour a 10-year contract with Corus' Teesside Cast Products, which accounted for 78% of the plant's operations. Corus' chief executive, Kirby Adams, said he was extremely disappointed that the consortium members had taken this action. Business Secretary Peter Mandelson said it is essential that Corus does everything it can legally, and with the government's assistance, to reinstate the agreement. British Prime Minister Gordon Brown said the government was doing everything in its power to ensure that the contract is upheld. Mandelson also said the government was not prepared to reconcile itself to the inevitable closure of the plant. The leader of Redcar and Cleveland Council, Councillor George Dunning, described the announcement as being hit by a mini earthquake. Liberal Democrats including Simon Hughes, Fiona Hall, and Stephen Hughes MEP supported the idea that the government should subsidise wages at the plant on a temporary basis. Hughes and Hall suggested the government should apply to the EU's European Globalisation Fund. Adams said the move could bring to an end a heritage of steelmaking at Teesside. A 90-day consultation period is due to begin, Corus said. Corus' owner, Tata Steel, is also facing difficulties with another UK operation, automobile company Jaguar Land Rover.

Organizers have scheduled a Conference of the Americas focused on Wikimedia in the Americas for May 15-18, 2008, at the Georgia Institute of Technology in Atlanta, Georgia. The planning followed Atlanta's unsuccessful bid to host Wikimania 2008, which was awarded to Alexandria, Egypt.

One organizer, an unpaid intern at the Wikimedia Foundation offices in St. Petersburg, Florida, said planning discussions began before the Wikimania host location was announced. The conference will cover Wikimedia and the free culture movement in relation to communities in North America, including the United States and Canada, and Latin America. The Wikimedia Foundation and Wikimedia Argentina have received proposals for endorsement, with decisions pending. Georgia Tech, the Public Journalism Network, and the Carolina Open Source Initiative are sponsoring the conference.

The selection of Alexandria as the Wikimania 2008 site prompted discussion on public mailing lists regarding safety, free speech, and the jury's decision process.

reconstructed_article: Corus, the world's fifth largest steel producer, announced on Friday that it may be forced to mothball its steelworks in Teesside, England, threatening the jobs of 1,920 employees. Corus may be forced to close its Teesside operations because a consortium has refused to honour a 10-year contract with Corus' Teesside Cast Products, which accounted for 78% of the plant's operations. Corus' chief executive, Kirby Adams, said he was extremely disappointed that the consortium members had taken this action. Business Secretary Peter Mandelson said it is essential that Corus does everything it can legally, and with the government's assistance, to reinstate the agreement. British Prime Minister Gordon Brown said the government was doing everything in its power to ensure that the contract is upheld. Mandelson also said the government was not prepared to reconcile itself to the inevitable closure of the plant. The leader of Redcar and Cleveland Council, Councillor George Dunning, described the announcement as being hit by a mini earthquake. Liberal Democrats including Simon Hughes, Fiona Hall, and Stephen Hughes MEP supported the idea that the government should subsidise wages at the plant on a temporary basis. Hughes and Hall suggested the government should apply to the EU's European Globalisation Fund. Adams said the move could bring to an end a proud heritage of steelmaking at Teesside. Corus said a 90-day consultation period is due to begin. Corus' owner, Tata Steel, is also facing difficulties with another UK operation, automobile company Jaguar Land Rover.

On February 2, 2008, approximately 100 people gathered in Orlando, Florida, to protest against the Church of Scientology. The protest was organized by the Internet-based group Anonymous as part of its Project Chanology movement. Anonymous formed the movement in response to what the group viewed as suppression of information on the Internet by the Church of Scientology. The group was initially motivated by the Church of Scientology's attempts to remove a promotional video featuring Scientologist Tom Cruise from the Internet. The Church of Scientology issued legal complaints to YouTube and Gawker; YouTube removed the video, but Gawker refused to remove it.

Project Chanology participants took down several Scientology websites in mid-January using denial-of-service attacks. The group organized a series of protests outside Church of Scientology centers worldwide on February 10, 2008, with at least 217 protests expected across cities including New York City, Montreal, Houston, London, Melbourne, and Los Angeles.

Protesters in Orlando held signs with messages including "Knowledge is Free Scientology Isn't," "Who Is Xenu?", "www.xenu.net," and "Honk if you hate Scientology." reconstructed_article:
On Tuesday, the World Bank released the 2012 World Development Report on Gender Equality and Development. Regarding Iceland, the report suggests that mandatory paid parental leave for mothers and fathers has played an important role in changing norms. Parents have nine months of government-mandated leave: three for the mother, three for the father, and three to distribute between them, paid at 80% of wages. The report describes changes in gender relations in Iceland as promising in terms of impact at work and home.

Icelandic boys' and girls' mathematics test scores were nearly identical, around 510, with boys slightly higher. Girls outperformed boys on literacy, approximately 525 to 480. Girls' mathematics performance was similar to Estonia, Germany, and Belgium; literacy performance was similar to Sweden, Poland, Switzerland, Estonia, and Belgium.

Iceland's mortality rate per 1,000 people aged 15–60 was 56, compared to the United States at 107, China at 113, India at 213, Iraq at 285, Afghanistan at 479, Malawi at 481, and Zimbabwe at 772. The report cites Iceland not being in a conflict or HIV/AIDS-affected country as a reason.

Iceland was one of 23 countries with over 30% female parliamentary representation, alongside Rwanda, Argentina, Cuba, Finland, the Netherlands, and Sweden. In the mid-1990s, only 5 countries met this threshold. The report cites the 1983 creation of an all-women's political party as increasing attention to women's issues.

Icelandic women in both private and public sectors earn approximately 22% less than men.

reconstructed_article:
An 11-year-old girl in California faces felony assault charges after throwing a stone at a group of boys who had been throwing water balloons at her.

In April, Maribel Cuevas was taken into custody by Fresno police and spent five days in a detention center after throwing the object at the group of boys as she walked down a sidewalk. A 9-year-old boy was struck by the stone and suffered a head wound requiring medical attention.

Since her release, Cuevas has spent one month under house arrest while awaiting court proceedings. Her lawyer, Richard Beshwate, told the BBC: "They [Fresno police] are treating her like a violent parole offender. It's not a felony, it's an 11-year-old acting like an 11-year-old."

Fresno Police Sergeant Anthony Martinez told reporters: "We responded. We determined a felony assault had taken place and the officers took the actions that were necessary."

Cuevas is due back in court next month on felony assault charges. During her five-day detention in juvenile hall, she received one 30-minute visit from her parents. She was then placed under 30 days of house arrest and required to wear an electronic monitoring bracelet, which allowed her to attend school.

Cuevas, who knows very little English, said the boy initiated the conflict; the boy also admitted as much.
